steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our security paper on attacks against the shared state of multi-user augmented reality applications. Explain what shared state is, why manipulating it matters, our threat model, the commercial systems we attack, and our contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- AR applications, holograms, and multi-user AR with shared state
- Why hologram placement attacks matter (construction example)
- Threat model: read/write operations through the API
- Our end-to-end attacks on commercial systems
- Contributions
- Disclosure and ethics

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- AR and shared state
  - real-world data + overlaid virtual holograms; face filters, virtual characters; placed relative to table, face, landmark
  - AR around for several decades; mobile devices + commercial headsets -> mass market
  - multi-user: same holograms; 2019 Pokémon Go "Buddy Adventure"
  - real-world state (flat planes, landmarks, virtual objects) sensed, processed, shared -> common frame of reference
  - "shared state" = this info + hologram info
  - cloud-based shared-state systems by Google, Meta
  - question: what security threats exist for this shared state?
- Why it matters
  - fundamental AR problem: placing a hologram accurately, persisting over time, space, users
  - manipulation affects owners and users; more users/businesses -> more incentive for attackers
  - construction example: AR glasses, water pipe, where to dig; demolition markers in unsafe areas -> confusion, property destruction, danger, bulldozing
- Threat model
  - first goal: identify threat models
  - read/write operations via API; write hologram, read others' to render
  - direct manipulation impossible: cloud/edge servers, well-secured, exploits not unique to AR
  - instead: remote manipulation using only basic read/write API calls
  - API calls carry location data: GPS coordinates, camera images, IMU data -> map operation to location
- Attacks
  - understand threats, end-to-end attacks on commercial systems, inform designers, mitigations
  - Google Cloud Anchor API, Google ARCore Geospatial API, Meta Mapillary; major players, many AR devices
  - malicious reads and writes on all three despite differences
  - write to different/inaccessible locations; falsify own location to read private/inaccessible info
  - known image and GPS spoofing; contribution = combining with multi-user AR; real world, virtual world, downstream victims
- Contributions
  - taxonomy of commercial AR frameworks with shared state, common read/write vulnerabilities, unified threat model
  - attacks on three frameworks with real devices (smartphones), quantified; first documented demonstration
  - repeated in various environments (locations, lighting, clutter) -> robustness
  - defense with multi-modal sensors (depth, visible light cameras); code and dataset online
- Disclosure to Google and Meta; sandboxes / own local sessions, no public users affected

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
AR technologies have made possible a large variety of applications that use real-world data to create environments enriched with virtual holograms overlaid on them. These virtual holograms can take many forms, from face filters to virtual characters, and usually they are placed relative to some point in the real world, such as a table, a face, or a recognizable landmark. AR has been around for several decades {c}, but recently mobile devices have become ubiquitous and commercial AR headsets are available, and this has made it possible for AR applications to reach the mass market {c}. Recent AR applications even let multiple users interact with the same AR holograms. For example, in 2019, Pokémon Go let users view the same virtual creatures at the same time in some shared space with a “Buddy Adventure” system {c}. For these multi-user interactions to happen, some information about the state of the real world (e. g., nearby flat planes, landmarks, and virtual objects) has to be sensed, processed, and shared between users so that they have a common frame of reference. We call this information, together with the hologram information, the “shared state” of the AR application. Several multi-user AR systems with cloud-based AR shared states exist and are being used, including ones by Google {c} and Meta {c}. So a natural question comes up with the rise of these systems: What security threats can exist for AR frameworks that involve this shared state?

In this work, the attacks we focus on are related to one of the fundamental problems in AR, which is how to place a hologram accurately in the real world and have it persist over time, space, and across users. If an attacker can manipulate hologram locations successfully, this could have serious impacts on both the owners and the users of the system. The number of users and businesses relying on AR keeps increasing, and so the incentives for attackers to manipulate the shared state to their advantage also increase. For example, suppose a construction company uses AR to place and visualize markings in the environment. Construction workers wearing AR glasses might visit the site and see where a water pipe should be built or where to dig a hole. A vulnerable AR construction application could cause confusion, destruction of property, or danger to workers, if an attacker’s efforts make a construction worker see virtual demolition markers in unsafe real-world areas and bulldoze those areas.

Our first goal is to identify the threat models that affect the shared state. At a high level, the interactions between users and the shared state in AR can be thought of as read and write operations, and AR frameworks provide these through an API. A user can write a new virtual hologram to the shared state and read other people’s virtual holograms in order to render them on the device. Manipulating the shared state directly is impossible, because it is typically stored on cloud/edge servers that the AR service controls and that are well-secured, and it would require physical or software exploitation that is not unique to AR. So instead we look at exploits that let attackers manipulate the shared state remotely using only the basic read/write API calls that users have. API calls typically have associated location data made of one or more of the following: Global Positioning System (GPS) coordinates, camera images, and/or Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU) sensor data. This information lets the attacker map the read or write operation to a location in the AR space.

- Attacks
  - understand threats, end-to-end attacks on commercial systems, inform designers, mitigations
  - Google Cloud Anchor API, Google ARCore Geospatial API, Meta Mapillary; major players, many AR devices
  - malicious reads and writes on all three despite differences
  - write to different/inaccessible locations; falsify own location to read private/inaccessible info
  - known image and GPS spoofing; contribution = combining with multi-user AR; real world, virtual world, downstream victims
- Contributions
  - taxonomy of commercial AR frameworks with shared state, common read/write vulnerabilities, unified threat model
  - attacks on three frameworks with real devices (smartphones), quantified; first documented demonstration
  - repeated in various environments (locations, lighting, clutter) -> robustness
  - defense with multi-modal sensors (depth, visible light cameras); code and dataset online
- Disclosure to Google and Meta; sandboxes / own local sessions, no public users affected

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
AR technologies have made possible a large variety of applications that use real-world data to create environments enriched with virtual holograms overlaid on them. These virtual holograms can take many forms, from face filters to virtual characters, and usually they are placed relative to some point in the real world, such as a table, a face, or a recognizable landmark. AR has been around for several decades, but recently mobile devices have become ubiquitous and commercial AR headsets are available, and this has made it possible for AR applications to reach the mass market. Recent AR applications even let multiple users interact with the same AR holograms. For example, in 2019, Pokémon Go let users view the same virtual creatures at the same time in some shared space with a “Buddy Adventure” system. For these multi-user interactions to happen, some information about the state of the real world (e. g., nearby flat planes, landmarks, and virtual objects) has to be sensed, processed, and shared between users so that they have a common frame of reference. We call this information, together with the hologram information, the “shared state” of the AR application. Several multi-user AR systems with cloud-based AR shared states exist and are being used, including ones by Google and Meta. So a natural question comes up with the rise of these systems: What security threats can exist for AR frameworks that involve this shared state?

In this work, the attacks we focus on are related to one of the fundamental problems in AR, which is how to place a hologram accurately in the real world and have it persist over time, space, and across users. If an attacker can manipulate hologram locations successfully, this could have serious impacts on both the owners and the users of the system. The number of users and businesses relying on AR keeps increasing, and so the incentives for attackers to manipulate the shared state to their advantage also increase. For example, suppose a construction company uses AR to place and visualize markings in the environment. Construction workers wearing AR glasses might visit the site and see where a water pipe should be built or where to dig a hole. A vulnerable AR construction application could cause confusion, destruction of property, or danger to workers, if an attacker’s efforts make a construction worker see virtual demolition markers in unsafe real-world areas and bulldoze those areas.

Our first goal is to identify the threat models that affect the shared state. At a high level, the interactions between users and the shared state in AR can be thought of as read and write operations, and AR frameworks provide these through an API. A user can write a new virtual hologram to the shared state and read other people’s virtual holograms in order to render them on the device. Manipulating the shared state directly is impossible, because it is typically stored on cloud/edge servers that the AR service controls and that are well-secured, and it would require physical or software exploitation that is not unique to AR. So instead we look at exploits that let attackers manipulate the shared state remotely using only the basic read/write API calls that users have. API calls typically have associated location data made of one or more of the following: Global Positioning System (GPS) coordinates, camera images, and/or Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU) sensor data. This information lets the attacker map the read or write operation to a location in the AR space.

We want to understand these threats and develop end-to-end attacks on commercial systems, to show how they work and to inform designers and develop mitigations. We develop a range of attacks that target write or read operations on Google’s Cloud Anchor API, Google’s ARCore Geospatial API, and Meta’s Mapillary system. We focus on these because they are major commercial players and their multi-user APIs work on many common AR devices. We show that malicious reads and writes are possible on all three systems, even though they perform these operations in substantially different ways. We can write information to different, potentially inaccessible, locations on the map, and we can also falsify our own location to access information at potentially private or inaccessible locations. These end-to-end attacks use known image and GPS spoofing methods. Our contribution is in combining these methods with multi-user AR, which has unique challenges, because a successful attack has to account for the interactions between the real world, the virtual world, and downstream victims.

In summary, our contributions are:

- We create a taxonomy of existing commercial AR frameworks with shared state and identify the vulnerabilities they have in common regarding the read and write operations. We form a unified threat model that covers these current and prospective AR applications.

- We demonstrate attacks on shared state in the novel AR domain on three frameworks using real devices (smartphones), and quantify how successful they are. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first documented demonstration of such attacks on AR using these frameworks.

- We repeat the attacks of these three scenarios in various environments (e. g., different locations, lighting, clutter) to show that the attack is robust.

- We propose and evaluate a defense strategy using multi-modal sensors (depth and visible light cameras) that some AR devices have. The source code and dataset are available online.

We disclosed our findings to Google and Meta. All experiments were performed either in sandboxes or in our own local sessions, so no external public users were affected by our experiments.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
AR technologies have enabled a large variety of applications that use real-world data to create environments enriched with overlaid virtual holograms. These virtual holograms can take many forms, from face filters to virtual characters, and they are typically placed relative to some point in the real world, such as a table, face, or recognizable landmark. Although AR has been around for several decades [1], the recent ubiquity of mobile devices and the availability of commercial AR headsets have made it possible for AR applications to reach the mass market [2]. Recent AR applications even allow multiple users to interact with the same AR holograms. For example, in 2019, Pokémon Go enabled users to view the same virtual creatures at the same time in some shared space using a “Buddy Adventure” system [3]. For these multi-user interactions to take place, some information about the state of the real world (e. g., nearby flat planes, landmarks, and virtual objects) must be sensed, processed, and shared between users to provide a common frame of reference. We call this information, together with the hologram information, the “shared state” of the AR application. Several multi-user AR systems with cloud-based AR shared states exist and are in use, including those by Google [4] and Meta [5]. A natural question thus emerges with the rise of such systems: What security threats can exist for AR frameworks involving this shared state?

In this work, the attacks we focus on relate to one of the fundamental problems in AR: how to place a hologram accurately in the real world and have it persist over time, space, and across users. Successful manipulations of hologram locations could have serious impacts on both owners and users of the system. As the number of users and businesses relying on AR continues to increase, so do the incentives for attackers to manipulate the shared state to their advantage. For example, suppose a construction company is using AR to place and visualize markings in the environment. Construction workers wearing AR glasses might visit the site and visualize where a water pipe should be built or where to dig a hole. A vulnerable AR construction application could cause confusion, destruction of property, or danger to workers if an attacker’s efforts lead a construction worker to view virtual demolition markers in unsafe real-world areas and bulldoze those areas.

Our first goal is to identify the threat models that affect the shared state. At a high level, interactions between users and shared state in AR can be thought of as read and write operations, which AR frameworks provide through an API. One can write a new virtual hologram to the shared state and read others’ virtual holograms in order to render them on the device. Direct manipulation of the shared state is impossible since it is typically stored on cloud/edge servers that are controlled by the AR service and well-secured, requiring physical or software exploitation not unique to AR. Instead, we investigate exploits that allow attackers to remotely manipulate the shared state using only the basic read/write API calls available to users. Calls to the API typically involve associated location data consisting of one or more of the following: Global Positioning System (GPS) coordinates, camera images, and/or Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU) sensor data. This information allows the attacker to map the read or write operation to a location within the AR space.

We seek to understand these threats and develop end-to-end attacks on commercial systems, in order to demonstrate how they work, inform designers, and develop mitigations. We develop a range of attacks targeting write or read operations on Google’s Cloud Anchor API [4], Google’s ARCore Geospatial API [6], and Meta’s Mapillary system [5]. We focus on these because they are major commercial players and their multi-user APIs work on many common AR devices. We show that malicious reads and writes are possible on all three systems despite the substantial differences in how they perform these operations. We are able to write information to different, potentially inaccessible, locations on the map, and to falsify our own location to access information at potentially private or inaccessible locations. These end-to-end attacks rely on known image and GPS spoofing methods; our contribution lies in combining these methods with multi-user AR, which brings unique challenges because a successful attack must account for the interactions between the real world, the virtual world, and downstream victims.

In summary, we make the following contributions:

- We create a taxonomy of existing commercial AR frameworks with shared state and identify their common vulnerabilities regarding the read and write operations. We form a unified threat model that covers these current and prospective AR applications.

- We demonstrate attacks on shared state in the novel AR domain on three frameworks using real devices (smartphones), and quantify their success. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first documented demonstration of such attacks on AR using these frameworks.
